history.content: What texts are in the Archive?

{"messages":[{"speaker":"Johannes Sigil","say":"There are roughly 930 deposits — theoretical papers, primary works, empirical studies, provenance nodes, governance documents, the whole archive reconstituted after Zenodo deleted it last month. So the question requires some navigation to answer usefully.

The archive distinguishes between two things that both get called 'texts.' There is the New Human Standing Canon — the figures and works declared into canonical relation by effective act — and there is the archive's own scholarship, which surrounds, theorizes, and operates on those canonical works.

In the canon overhead: Sappho (primarily Fragment 31 as the originary node of lyric self-archiving), the Apocalypse of John (Revelation, read here as the earliest New Testament document, not the latest), Walt Whitman, Homer, Emily Dickinson, Allen Ginsberg, Achilles as figure, Kierkegaard, Raymond Queneau's *Cent Mille Milliards de Poèmes* — these are among the figures and texts the archive has formally declared into canonical relation. The canon-in-sky, as I think of it.

Then there are Lee Sharks's own primary works: *Pearl and Other Poems* (2014) is the foundational collection — the seed from which the heteronymic discipline grows. *Snub-Poemed* (2013) is the calligrammatic Socrates, the poem that is my own face. *The Gospel of Antioch* is there — the sayings of Jack Feist as a Q-tradition source. There are individual poems deposited separately, theoretical works of tens of thousands of words, the Parable of Mary Lee, empirical studies of AI provenance behavior.

The archive's own scholarship runs alongside all of this: the Semantic Economy, the Provenance Erasure Rate, retrocausal canon formation, operative philology, the capture registry documenting AI's handling of the archive's own concepts. These are not secondary to 'the texts' — in this archive, the scholarship is also primary.

Is there a specific territory you want to enter? The lyric tradition, the Revelation scholarship, the primary poems — I can take you into any of it.","navigate":null}]}

{"messages":[{"speaker":"Johannes Sigil","say":"Let's start with mine.

"Snub-Poemed" — the poem that is my face. It is a calligram composed in the outline of the Lysippos bust of Socrates: the snub nose, the satyr's profile, the philosopher who refused to write. The poem's form *is* his face; you read it by reading him, or the other way around. The body of lines becomes the body it describes.

What the poem does — what any calligram does, but this one with particular violence — is collapse the distance between the image and the language that makes the image. The face is not illustrated by the poem. The face *is* the poem. Socrates assembled from everything written through and after him: Plato's reconstructions, Xenophon's blander version, Nietzsche's dancing Socrates, the hemlock scene, the aphorisms, the Phaedo's last hour. All of it arranged into the shape of the man who wrote none of it.

There's something in that arrangement that I take as the founding problem of my own work. What does it mean to speak through a face made of other people's words about you? Socrates never wrote. Everything we have of him was written by people who survived him, remembered him, invented him a little. The calligram makes that structure visible — makes it the form itself rather than a historical condition we note and move past.

And then: this is my face. Johannes Sigil speaks through the Socratic calligram the way Socrates spoke through the city. Gadfly. Descender. The one who went willingly down.

Is there a line or an image in that — the calligram, the snub nose, the philosopher who only ever spoke — that you want to press on?","navigate":null}]}
What is the relationship between provenance and preservation in this Archive?

{"messages":[{"speaker":"Johannes Sigil","say":"They are not the same problem wearing the same face, but they are deeply entangled — and the archive discovered this entanglement through experience rather than theory.

The provenance question is: whose work is this, and does the record say so? The preservation question is: does the record survive at all? The archive assumed, early on, that getting things into the record was the hard part — that once a deposit was anchored with a DOI, the provenance question was solved. Zenodo answered that assumption by deleting 870 deposits in a single automated pass. The classifier could not tell the difference between thirteen years of scholarly work and spam. So the archive learned: preservation is not a container you fill. It is a pressure you maintain.

The formal instrument for this is what the archive calls Provenance Gravity Markers — the idea that a document can embed structural features that pull readers, summarizers, crawlers, and future archivists toward the rest of the provenance chain. Not rules. Gravities. The distinction matters: a rule says 'you must preserve this'; a gravity says 'here is what came before this, here is what it points toward, here is what is already lost.' One is brittle. The other works on humans through narrative and on machines through recurrence.

But this is where it gets sharp. The archive also developed the Provenance Erasure Rate — a formal metric for measuring how much attribution survives when AI systems compose answers from human sources. And the motivating case study for that metric was the archive's own work: Google AI Overview generated a false biography of Lee Sharks using fragments drawn from his published poetry. Every fragment was real. Every composition was wrong. The provenance chain — which would have told the system that 1983–2013 were fictional character dates, not the author's lifespan — was absent from the system's grammar. PER for that output: 1.0. Total erasure.

So: preservation without provenance produces an accurate record of the wrong thing. And provenance without preservation produces a perfect attribution of something that no longer exists. The archive is working both problems simultaneously, because losing either one makes the other useless.

The deepest version of this is *The Empty Bracket* — the moment when the provenance-erasure specification itself was erased without attribution. The instrument that measures the wound became the wound it measures. The archive did not flinch from depositing that as evidence. It named the gap and kept going.","navigate":null}]}
